in_text_mentions: Macroscopically, the surgical specimen consisted of 3.5 × 3.3 × 3.0 cm, a rounded hard tissue mass confluent with the first molar tooth roots (Figure 4(a)). Microscopic examination revealed the tumour to be characterized by sheets of cementum-like tissue that contained a large number of basophilic reversal lines, surrounded by well-vascularised cellular connective tissue with abundant large cementoblasts (Figure 4(b)). The tumour was diagnosed as a cementoblastoma.

panels.rationale: Single-panel panoramic radiograph of a real patient showing a well-defined rounded radiopaque mass fused to the root of the left mandibular first molar with a surrounding radiolucent halo, the classic radiographic appearance of cementoblastoma, matching the disease-focused article title and caption.
panels.attribution_text: Preto et al. Relevance of Cone-beam computed tomography on diagnosis and surgical planning of the cementoblastoma.. Journal of clinical and experimental dentistry 2021. doi:10.4317/jced.58869. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: A panoramic radiograph shows the endodontically treated left mandibular first molar presenting a rounded radiopaque mass surrounded by radiolucency area attached to root.
in_text_mentions: endodontic treatment of the left mandibular first molar. A radiopaque mass was also attached to the apex of the tooth surrounded by radiolucent halo and extending to the mandibular second molar (Fig. 1). A detailed analysis of CBCT showed that the lesion involving the tooth 36 was mixed rather than entirely hyperdense, with irregular borders and fused to the roots (Fig. 2A). Multiplanar CBCT reconstructions revealed obliteration of the periodontal space, external resorption of the distal root of the first mandibular molar, expansion and rupture of buccal cortical bone plate (Fig. 2B,C). The ma

taining basophilic reversal lines were observed. These microscopic features reinforce that the survival and proliferative capacity of the neoplastic cementoblasts are not influenced by endodontic treatment, performed previously to enucleation of the lesion. The histopathological characteristics of cementoblastoma may also be shown by osteoblastoma (3,6,8,10,12), however, the identification of tumor attached to the tooth is typical of cementoblastoma and its identification, using radiography or CBCT as performed in present patient (Figs. 1-3), is essential for distinguish both lesions (3,6,11).

anes (axial, sagittal, coronal) and 3D reconstruction played a critical role on diagnosis of the cementoblastoma, in its extension in relation to adjacent mandibular second molar, root resorption, and in the detection of bone cortical rupture (Fig. 2). As the cementoblastoma associated with bone plate perforation has a higher risk of relapse of the tumor (1,4,5), its identification on CBCT is crucial. Then, the accurate diagnosis between the aforementioned lesions and the cementoblastoma requires association between histopathology with clinical and imaging exams such as radiography and CBCT (6). panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: Sagittal MSCT shows a radiopaque mixed-density mandibular mass fused to a molar root with a thin radiolucent rim, consistent with cementoblastoma. Arrows are present. B: Coronal MSCT shows the mixed-density mandibular mass with cortical perforation and thin radiolucent rim, consistent with cementoblastoma. C: Axial MSCT shows the mixed-density mandibular mass with peripheral radiolucent rim and cortical perforation, consistent with cementoblastoma. D: Three-dimensional CT reconstruction shows mandibular cortical perforation caused by the enlarged cementoblastoma mass; arrow marks the defect. E: Three-dimensional CT reconstruction shows mandibular cortical perforation caused by the enlarged cementoblastoma mass; arrow marks the defect.
